lead: Many circuits are not one resistor. They are groups in series, groups in parallel, and groups inside groups. Two reduction rules replace each group by one equivalent resistance. The voltage divider gives one series element's voltage; the current divider gives one parallel branch's current. With these, a 12 V supply feeding a small resistor network becomes one resistance, one source current, and a few branch values. Phone chargers, LED strings, sensor dividers and current shunts use the same arithmetic. The rules come from Ohm's law plus Kirchhoff's laws.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for R, L, C and 1.3 for Ohm's law, KCL and KVL.

blocks.text: Two elements are in series when the same current must pass through both, with no other path at the joining node. Resistors R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, ..., in series add:

blocks.where: R<sub>eq</sub> is the one resistance that would draw the same current from the same source; each R is in ohms (Ω).

blocks.text: Two elements are in parallel when they share the same two nodes, so both have the same voltage. For resistors in parallel:

blocks.where: R<sub>eq</sub> is the equivalent resistance in ohms; each R is a branch resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: For exactly two resistors this becomes R<sub>eq</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> × R<sub>2</sub> / (R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>). For n equal resistors of value R, R<sub>eq</sub> = R/n. The parallel equivalent is always smaller than the smallest branch resistance.

items: Mark nodes and label each resistor.
Combine a clear series chain by adding.
Combine a clear parallel group by reciprocals or the two-resistor form.
Redraw with the new single resistor.
Repeat until one source and one R<sub>eq</sub> remain.

blocks.text: Reduction is valid while the group really shares one current (series) or one voltage (parallel). If a dependent source or a tapped connection makes that shared current or voltage depend on something outside the group, replace the group only with care. KCL and KVL from 1.3 justify the rules. Some syllabi call this network reduction.
A voltage divider is a series chain. The same current I flows through every resistor. Ohm's law gives I = V<sub>s</sub>/R<sub>total</sub>. The voltage across R<sub>x</sub> is:

blocks.where: V<sub>x</sub> is the voltage across R<sub>x</sub> in volts (V); V<sub>s</sub> is the source voltage in volts; R<sub>total</sub> is the series sum in ohms; R<sub>x</sub> is one series resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: For two series resistors, V<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub>). The larger resistor takes the larger share of voltage.
A current divider is a parallel group. The same voltage sits across every branch. For two resistors carrying total current I<sub>s</sub>:

blocks.where: I<sub>1</sub> is the current in R<sub>1</sub> in amperes (A); I<sub>2</sub> is the current in R<sub>2</sub> in A; I<sub>s</sub> is the total current entering the pair in A; R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> are in ohms.

blocks.text: Notice the reversal: the current in R<sub>1</sub> uses R<sub>2</sub> on top. The smaller resistance takes the larger current. For more than two branches use conductance G = 1/R, in siemens (S): I<sub>k</sub> = I<sub>s</sub> G<sub>k</sub>/G<sub>total</sub>, where G<sub>total</sub> = G<sub>1</sub> + G<sub>2</sub> + ... is the sum of the branch conductances. Divider rules save solving KCL and KVL when only one branch value is wanted. Sensor voltage dividers, LED current sharing and shunt resistors use them daily.

sections.h3: Inductors, capacitors and where reduction stops

blocks.text: The same series and parallel patterns apply to ideal inductors and capacitors, but with swapped roles. From the V-I relations in 1.1:

So series inductors add, parallel inductors use reciprocals. Parallel capacitors add, series capacitors use reciprocals. These results are for ideal components; real coils have resistance and real capacitors have leakage, handled later.

Reduction stops at a bridge or ladder where no pair is simply series or parallel. Use star-delta in 1.6, source transformation in 1.7, or mesh and nodal analysis in Unit 2. Time-domain RL and RC behaviour is Unit 5. AC impedance dividers are Unit 3.

spec.title: Reduce to one resistor
spec.aria: Three boxes reduce the 12 Ω and 6 Ω parallel pair to 4 Ω, add the 6 Ω series resistor to get 10 Ω, and apply divider rules to get 4.8 V and branch currents 0.4 A and 0.8 A.

examples.question: A 12 V source feeds R<sub>1</sub> = 6 Ω in series with a parallel pair R<sub>2</sub> = 12 Ω and R<sub>3</sub> = 6 Ω. Find the equivalent resistance, the source current, the voltage across the parallel pair, and the current in each parallel resistor.
steps: The parallel pair R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> has R<sub>23</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>/(R<sub>2</sub>+R<sub>3</sub>) = (12×6)/(12+6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω.
Add the series R<sub>1</sub>: R<sub>eq</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>23</sub> = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω.
This current flows through R<sub>1</sub>. Voltage across the parallel pair is V<sub>23</sub> = I<sub>s</sub>R<sub>23</sub> = 1.2×4 = 4.8 V. Check: V<sub>1</sub> = 1.2×6 = 7.2 V; 7.2+4.8=12 V.
Current in R<sub>2</sub>: I<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>23</sub>/R<sub>2</sub> = 4.8/12 = 0.4 A.
Current in R<sub>3</sub>: I<sub>3</sub> = V<sub>23</sub>/R<sub>3</sub> = 4.8/6 = 0.8 A. Check: 0.4+0.8=1.2 A.
examples.answer: R<sub>eq</sub> = 10 Ω; source current = 1.2 A; parallel-pair voltage = 4.8 V; I<sub>2</sub> = 0.4 A; I<sub>3</sub> = 0.8 A.
examples.check:
R1=6
R2=12
R3=6
Vs=12
R23=R2*R3/(R2+R3)
Req=R1+R23
Is=Vs/Req
V23=Is*R23
I2=V23/R2
I3=V23/R3
print(R23)
print(Req)
print(Is)
print(V23)
print(I2)
print(I3)

traps: Using R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub>) for the current through R<sub>2</sub> in a parallel pair. The current divider is reversed: I<sub>2</sub> = I<sub>s</sub> R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub>).
Adding parallel resistors directly: 12 Ω with 6 Ω is not 18 Ω; use the reciprocal or product-over-sum.
Using R<sub>eq</sub> = R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub> for a group that shares two nodes. Series addition needs the same current, not just same drawing line.
Applying a voltage divider to a parallel group. The divider formula is for series resistors carrying one common current.
Writing series capacitors as C<sub>1</sub>+C<sub>2</sub> or parallel inductors as L<sub>1</sub>+L<sub>2</sub>. These use reciprocals.

quiz.q: State the condition for two resistors to be in series and the condition to be in parallel.
quiz.a: Series: the same current must pass through both, with no other path at the joining node. Parallel: both share the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage.

quiz.q: Why does the current divider put the other resistance on top?
quiz.a: The branch currents are inversely proportional to branch resistance because the voltage is common. With V = I<sub>s</sub>R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub>), I<sub>1</sub> = V/R<sub>1</sub> simplifies to I<sub>s</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub>). The smaller resistance takes the larger current.

quiz.q: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected as two in parallel, and that pair in series with the third, across 12 V. Find R<sub>eq</sub>, source current, and voltage across the parallel pair.
quiz.a: Parallel pair = 6×6/(6+6) = 3 Ω. R<sub>eq</sub> = 3+6 = 9 Ω. Source current = 12/9 = 1.33 A. Voltage across the parallel pair = 1.33×3 = 4 V.

quiz.q: A 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor are in parallel across 24 V. A student says the 4 Ω branch has 16 V. Identify the error and give the correct branch currents.
quiz.a: Parallel branches have the same voltage, so both have 24 V. I<sub>4</sub> = 24/4 = 6 A; I<sub>8</sub> = 24/8 = 3 A. The 16 V answer wrongly applies a series voltage-divider idea.

quiz.q: 10 V is applied across 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series. Find the voltage across the 6 Ω resistor.
quiz.a: R<sub>total</sub> = 4+6 = 10 Ω. Current = 10/10 = 1 A. Voltage across 6 Ω = 1×6 = 6 V.

quiz.q: In a parallel pair R<sub>1</sub> = 2 Ω, R<sub>2</sub> = 8 Ω, total current I<sub>s</sub> = 5 A. Find I<sub>1</sub> using the correct current divider and using the wrong ratio I<sub>s</sub>R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub>+R<sub>2</sub>). State which is wrong.
quiz.a: Correct: I<sub>1</sub> = 5×8/(2+8) = 4 A. Wrong ratio: 5×2/10 = 1 A. The wrong ratio gives the smaller branch the smaller current, but the 2 Ω branch must carry more current than the 8 Ω branch.

beyond: Not for the exam. On a PCB, divider rules estimate bias points before simulation and current dividers size shunt resistors. Power engineers use reduction to check voltage drop along a distribution line; IC designers use it in analog layout parasitic checks. Search next for ladder network reduction, Thevenin equivalent from dividers, and impedance divider for AC. The same rules reappear as Y-Δ transforms and two-port parameter conversions.
